stem: A support team must classify each incoming ticket into one of five queues and then draft a reply using a queue-specific template. The steps are always the same, the categories are fixed, and auditors require predictable behavior. Which design best fits?

options.text: A fully autonomous agent that decides its own steps and tools for every ticket.
A workflow: a classification call that routes to a fixed, queue-specific drafting prompt.
A supervisor agent that spawns a new subagent for every ticket to explore options.
A single prompt containing all five templates and letting the model choose freely.

rationale: When the steps are known in advance and predictability matters, a workflow (here, routing) gives control and auditability. Agents fit open-ended problems where the path cannot be hard-coded.

why_wrong.A: Autonomy adds cost and unpredictability the problem does not need.
why_wrong.C: Subagent hierarchies help with broad, parallelizable exploration, not with a fixed two-step pipeline.
why_wrong.D: It works sometimes but loses the explicit, testable routing step auditors want.

source.excerpt: When more complexity is warranted, workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks

stem: You are writing a custom agent loop with the Messages API. After a call returns, what should the loop check to decide whether to execute tools and call the model again?

options.text: Whether the response text contains the word "done" or a similar completion phrase.
Whether stop_reason is "tool_use"; if so, run the tools and return tool_result blocks.
Whether usage.output_tokens is greater than zero, meaning the model produced output.
Whether the HTTP status code is 200, meaning the turn completed successfully.

rationale: A stop_reason of tool_use means the model is waiting for tool results. The loop executes the requested tools, returns tool_result blocks referencing each tool_use_id, and calls again until another stop_reason (such as end_turn) arrives.

why_wrong.A: Text matching is fragile and not how the API signals tool requests.
why_wrong.C: Almost every response has output tokens; it says nothing about tool requests.
why_wrong.D: A 200 only means the request succeeded, not that the turn is finished.

source.excerpt: Claude responds with stop_reason: "tool_use" and one or more tool_use blocks.

stem: A research agent runs for hundreds of turns. Its context fills with large raw tool outputs, and quality degrades late in the session. Which TWO techniques directly address this?

options.text: Prune or clear stale tool results from the context once they have been used.
Delegate deep-dive searches to subagents that return only condensed findings.
Increase max_tokens so the model can write longer answers.
Raise temperature to make the agent explore more options.
Repeat the system prompt at the end of every user turn.

rationale: Context bloat is solved by keeping less in the main window: clearing consumed tool outputs, and isolating exploration in subagents whose own windows absorb the raw data while only summaries return.

why_wrong.C: max_tokens limits output length; it does not shrink the input context.
why_wrong.D: Temperature affects sampling, not context size.
why_wrong.E: Repeating instructions adds tokens and does not remove the bloat.

source.excerpt: One of the safest lightest touch forms of compaction is tool result clearing

options.text: Use the Agent SDK to run the Claude Code agent from the team's own application process.
Drive every support request through the interactive Claude Code CLI in a terminal.
Call the Claude API via the Client SDK and hand-write the full tool loop.
Use Managed Agents with an Anthropic-hosted harness configured via the API.

rationale: The Agent SDK is the library for embedding Claude Code's agent in your own Python or TypeScript application in a process you operate. It ships Claude Code's capabilities, including built-in tools, permissions, sessions, and hooks, so the team gets the full agent rather than rebuilding one.

source.excerpt: A library that runs the Claude Code binary

stem: A product team is building a Python support application and wants to embed Claude Code's full agent, including its built-in file tools, permissions, sessions, and hooks, inside a process the team operates. Which approach BEST fits this requirement?

why_wrong.B: The CLI is tempting because it has the full agent, but it is built for interactive terminal use, not for embedding in an application process.
why_wrong.C: The Client SDK tempts with full control, but it means writing the tool loop yourself instead of getting Claude Code's capabilities.
why_wrong.D: Managed Agents tempt with zero hosting effort, but the harness runs hosted, not inside a process the team operates.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that inspects each Bash call and denies destructive commands.
A PostToolUse hook that reviews shell output and warns after risky commands run.
A system prompt instruction telling the model never to run destructive commands.
A SessionStart hook that injects a safe-shell reminder into the session context.

rationale: Hooks run custom code at key points in the agent lifecycle, and blocking dangerous operations before they execute is a core hook use case. A PreToolUse hook fires before the tool call executes and can deny it, giving a deterministic guardrail independent of model judgment.

source.excerpt: Block dangerous operations before they execute, like destructive shell commands or unauthorized file access

stem: A DevOps team runs a coding agent with shell access. They need a deterministic guardrail that stops destructive shell commands, such as recursive deletes, before they execute, without relying on the model's judgment. Which mechanism BEST provides this?

why_wrong.B: PostToolUse review sounds diligent, but it runs after the command succeeds, so the damage is already done.
why_wrong.C: A prompt instruction is cheap to add, but it still relies on the model obeying it rather than enforcing anything.
why_wrong.D: Startup context sounds helpful, but SessionStart hooks only add context and have no blocking control.

options.text: Streaming Input Mode, a persistent interactive session with queued messages and live feedback.
Single Message Input with one-shot queries that resume stored session state each time.
A fresh stateless query per message with transcript persistence disabled entirely.
Forking the session before every message to preserve each alternative branch.

rationale: Streaming Input Mode is the persistent, interactive session option: it supports queued messages that process sequentially with the ability to interrupt, image uploads, and context that persists across turns. One-shot queries fit single prompts, not an interactive assistant with follow-ups and interruptions.

source.excerpt: a persistent, interactive session

stem: A startup is building an interactive pair-programming assistant where a developer sends follow-up messages, uploads screenshots of errors, and interrupts long-running work mid-turn. The session must keep conversation context across turns naturally. Which input approach BEST meets these requirements?

why_wrong.B: One-shot queries with resume sound simpler, but they fit single prompts, not an interactive session with interruptions.
why_wrong.C: Stateless queries tempt with simplicity, but they discard the cross-turn context the assistant requires.
why_wrong.D: Forking sounds safe, but forks create alternative branches instead of one continuous interactive session.

options.text: Run sessions in a self-hosted sandbox on the bank's own infrastructure.
Run sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox configured through the API.
Embed the agent with the Agent SDK subprocess model on developer laptops.
Route all turns through the Client SDK beta tool runner on shared runners.

rationale: Managed Agents is a hosted harness that runs the agent loop, and sessions can run either in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or in a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure. Choosing the self-hosted sandbox keeps the hosted-harness model while satisfying the requirement that code never leaves the bank's VPC.

source.excerpt: A hosted agent harness that runs the agent loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure.

stem: A bank wants an Anthropic-hosted agent harness, but compliance requires all agent sessions to execute on the bank's own infrastructure so code never leaves its VPC. Which Managed Agents configuration BEST satisfies this constraint?

why_wrong.B: The Anthropic-managed sandbox is the default hosted path, but it runs sessions on Anthropic compute, violating the VPC constraint.
why_wrong.C: The SDK subprocess model tempts as self-operated, but laptops are not a compliant sandbox and drop the hosted harness.
why_wrong.D: The beta tool runner sounds lightweight, but it is a client-side loop, not a hosted harness with sandbox choice.

options.text: The ResultMessage subtype, which reports success versus limit outcomes for the run.
The count of AssistantMessage objects, treating more than ten as a success.
The presence of a SystemMessage init event, which confirms task completion.
Whether any StreamEvent arrived, treating raw deltas as proof of completion.

rationale: ResultMessage marks the end of the agent loop and carries the final text, token usage, cost, and session ID. Its subtype field is the documented signal for whether the task succeeded or hit a limit, so branching on it is the reliable programmatic check.

source.excerpt: Check the subtype field to determine whether the task succeeded or hit a limit.

stem: A team built an Agent SDK integration that streams messages for a refactoring task. After the run, they need to programmatically determine whether the task succeeded or stopped early because it hit a turn or cost limit. What should the code check?

why_wrong.B: Message counts feel quantitative, but AssistantMessage volume reflects chattiness, not whether the run succeeded or hit a limit.
why_wrong.C: The init event is tempting as a lifecycle signal, but it carries session metadata at startup, not the final outcome.
why_wrong.D: StreamEvents tempt as liveness proof, but they are raw partial-message deltas with no success-versus-limit verdict.

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that denies writes to protected config paths before they run.
A hook requiring human approval before sensitive actions like database writes.
A Notification hook that plays a sound after each migration finishes.
A SessionStart hook adding a policy reminder to the session context.
A PostCompact hook logging a summary line whenever compaction occurs.

rationale: PreToolUse hooks fire before a tool call executes and can block it, which enforces path protection deterministically. Requiring human approval for sensitive actions like database writes is the other documented hook control, keeping risky operations gated regardless of what the model decides.

source.excerpt: Require human approval for sensitive actions like database writes or API calls

stem: A platform team operates an agent that can edit production configuration files and execute database migrations. They want deterministic controls that do not depend on model judgment. Select TWO hook-based controls that BEST meet this goal.

why_wrong.C: A completion sound feels like oversight, but it only notifies after the fact and blocks nothing.
why_wrong.D: A startup reminder sounds prudent, but SessionStart hooks only add context with no blocking control.
why_wrong.E: Compaction logging aids debugging, but it observes context management instead of gating risky actions.

options.text: Capture each customer's session ID and pass it to resume when they return.
Use continue on every request to pick up the most recent session.
Fork the most recent session daily and share the fork across customers.
Start each return with a fresh one-shot query and merge histories by hand.

rationale: Resume takes a specific session ID that the application tracks, and it is required when there are multiple sessions, such as one per user in a multi-user app. Continue only finds the most recent session in the directory, which would hand returning customers each other's conversations.

source.excerpt: Resume takes a specific session ID. You track the ID. Required when you have multiple sessions

stem: A SaaS company runs one long-lived agent conversation per customer inside a single server process. After a deployment restart, each returning customer must continue their own conversation, not the most recently active one. Which session approach BEST meets this requirement?

why_wrong.B: Continue is tempting because it needs no ID handling, but it resumes only the most recent session, mixing up customers.
why_wrong.C: A shared fork sounds efficient, but forks branch one session, so customers would still share state.
why_wrong.D: Fresh queries with manual merges sound clean, but they discard session continuity that resume provides.

options.text: Add a deny rule for Bash rm patterns, denied in every mode including bypass.
Drop Bash from allowed tools so the agent never sees any Bash command.
Add a hook asking the operator to approve every Bash call at runtime.
Set bypassPermissions mode and instruct the model to avoid deletions.

rationale: Deny rules for a command pattern stay denied in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions, while other Bash calls still fall through to the normal flow. That gives a mode-proof guarantee for deletions while preserving read-only shell use, which neither allow-lists nor approvals can promise.

source.excerpt: Calls matching rm * as written are denied in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions

stem: A security engineer must guarantee that a deployment agent can never run rm deletions via Bash, even if an operator later enables a permissive mode for a demo. The agent still needs Bash for read-only commands like ls and git status. Which configuration BEST guarantees this?

why_wrong.B: Trimming allowed tools sounds strict, but unlisted tools still exist and fall through to approval instead of being denied.
why_wrong.C: Per-call approval feels safe, but it depends on operator vigilance and can be bypassed along with the mode change.
why_wrong.D: Bypass mode with an instruction is the weakest option: it auto-approves calls and relies purely on model obedience.

options.text: Write a precise description, since Claude reads it to decide when to call it.
Return isError true with a composed message on database failures for recovery.
Leave the description empty so Claude calls the tool on every message.
Raise a raw unhandled exception so the loop crashes loudly on failure.
Allow-list the tool name without defining any schema or handler for it.

rationale: A custom tool's description is what Claude reads to decide when to call it, so precision there drives correct invocation timing. On failures, returning isError true composes the message Claude reads instead of surfacing a raw exception, letting the agent react and recover rather than crash.

source.excerpt: Description: what the tool does. Claude reads this to decide when to call it.

stem: A team is building a custom lookup_order tool for their Agent SDK agent. The tool must be invoked at the right moments and must let the agent recover gracefully when the order database is down. Select TWO design decisions that BEST achieve this.

why_wrong.C: An empty description tempts with maximum availability, but with no signal Claude cannot learn when the tool applies.
why_wrong.D: A loud crash feels honest, but a raw exception surfaces instead of the composed error Claude needs to react.
why_wrong.E: Allow-listing alone sounds sufficient, but without a schema and handler there is no tool for Claude to call.

options.text: The harness deletes the blocks itself, and client-stripped reasoning is lost forever.
The API deletes unreadable thinking blocks from the stored message history.
Thinking blocks never survive any model switch, so routing always destroys them.
Dropped thinking blocks are billed as input tokens, exhausting the context early.

rationale: The API drops unreadable thinking blocks before the prompt reaches the model but never edits the client's messages array, so the blocks stay in history and become readable again on return. Reasoning is lost for good only when the client removes the blocks itself, exactly what a harness that strips thinking on model switch does.

source.excerpt: lost for good only if your client removes the blocks itself, for example a harness that strips thinking on a model switch

stem: A team built a custom harness that routes turns across different Claude models to control cost. After adding a step that strips thinking blocks from history whenever the model changes, they notice degraded reasoning even when the conversation later returns to the original model. What is the MOST likely cause?

why_wrong.B: API-side dropping is real and tempting, but the API never edits your history, so its drops are reversible.
why_wrong.C: Total loss sounds plausible, but many switches preserve reasoning when the client keeps sending full history.
why_wrong.D: Billing blame is tempting, but dropped blocks are not billed and do not count toward input tokens.

options.text: Execute the requested tool, send the output back as a tool_result block, and repeat while the stop reason is tool_use.
Wait for the model to run the database query itself, then read the final answer from the same response.
Resend the original user message unchanged until the stop reason changes to end_turn.
Append the tool output as a new system prompt and restart the conversation from scratch.

rationale: Client-executed tools require the application to drive the loop, because the model only emits structured requests and never runs code itself. The canonical pattern repeats the request cycle while the stop reason is tool_use and exits on end_turn or another stop reason.

source.excerpt: In practice this reads as: while stop_reason == "tool_use", execute the tools and continue the conversation.

stem: A junior developer is building her first tool-using agent with the Claude API. She defines a database lookup tool, sends a user message with the tools array, and receives a response with stop_reason "tool_use". Which approach BEST completes the agent loop?

why_wrong.B: This tempts because server-executed tools do run without app code, but client tools never execute themselves, so waiting returns nothing.
why_wrong.C: Resending looks like a retry strategy, but without tool_result blocks the model simply repeats the same tool request.
why_wrong.D: Restarting feels clean, but it discards conversation state and the tool output never reaches the model in the required shape.

options.text: Define a reviewer subagent restricted to read-only tools so it can analyze the docs but never modify files.
Give the reviewer the full toolset and ask it politely in the prompt to avoid making any changes.
Run the review in the main agent conversation so every file edit stays visible for auditing.
Disable tool use entirely and paste each document into one giant user message for review.

rationale: Subagents can be limited to specific tools, which reduces the risk of unintended actions while preserving their ability to analyze. A read-only reviewer satisfies the safety requirement by construction rather than by persuasion.

source.excerpt: subagents can be limited to specific tools, reducing the risk of unintended actions

stem: A platform team adds a documentation-review step to their CI pipeline using the Claude Agent SDK. The reviewer must read docs and search for inconsistencies, but it must never modify files or run shell commands. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: A polite instruction sounds cooperative, but prompt text is not enforcement and the model can still call dangerous tools.
why_wrong.C: Visibility aids auditing, but running in the main conversation removes isolation and still permits accidental edits.
why_wrong.D: Disabling tools does prevent edits, but pasting whole docs bloats the main context and breaks on large doc sets.

options.text: Run style, security, and coverage checks as concurrent subagents so the gate finishes in the slowest-check time.
Let each check explore files inside its own subagent so only a concise verdict returns to the main chat.
Run the three checks sequentially in the main conversation to keep full file contents in shared context.
Merge all three checks into one giant system prompt so the model sees every rule at the same time.
Raise the sampling temperature so the reviewer explores more diverse and creative code paths.

rationale: Independent subtasks run concurrently finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum, which meets the speed requirement. Context isolation keeps each check's intermediate file reads inside its own subagent, so the parent receives concise verdicts instead of raw file contents.

source.excerpt: multiple subagents can run concurrently, so independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of all of them

stem: A release pipeline needs a review gate with three independent checks (style, security, test coverage). Each check reads many repository files, and the gate must finish as fast as possible without flooding the main conversation with file contents. Select TWO approaches that together BEST meet the requirement.

why_wrong.C: Sequential execution feels simpler, but it sums the check times and floods the main window with raw file contents.
why_wrong.D: One prompt looks efficient, but it mixes unrelated expertise into noise and loses both isolation and parallelism.
why_wrong.E: Higher temperature changes sampling randomness, which neither speeds up checks nor isolates their context.

options.text: Enable the memory tool so the agent records facts in memory files and reads them back on demand.
Prepend all prior transcripts to every request so the model never misses historical context.
Store customer history in the system prompt template shared across every customer.
Ask each customer to retype their full history at the start of every new session.

rationale: The memory tool stores and retrieves information across conversations in persistent memory files. Just-in-time retrieval keeps the active context focused on the current task instead of loading every prior transcript upfront, which is exactly what long-lived support sessions need.

source.excerpt: The memory tool lets Claude store and retrieve information across conversations in a directory of memory files.

stem: A SaaS company ships a support copilot. Customers return over many weeks, and the agent must recall each customer's earlier issues and past decisions without loading every prior transcript into the context window. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: Full transcripts seem thorough, but they bloat the active window and eventually overwhelm long-running sessions.
why_wrong.C: A shared template looks convenient, but it mixes customers' data together and leaks private history across accounts.
why_wrong.D: Re-asking guarantees fresh input, but it burdens the user and discards everything the agent already learned.

options.text: Enable context editing to clear consumed results while the agent saves progress summaries to memory files.
Disable all context management so no tool result is ever cleared from the conversation history.
Increase the output token limit so cleared results can always be regenerated from scratch.
Copy every tool result into the system prompt so that clearing cannot remove it.

rationale: Context editing can be combined with the memory tool: the agent writes essential information from tool results to memory files before those results are cleared. This preserves progress for long-running workflows that would otherwise exceed context limits, while keeping the active window lean.

source.excerpt: Claude can write essential information from tool results to memory files before those results are cleared

stem: A refactoring agent performs hundreds of file operations in one session. Early tool results become irrelevant, but the agent must retain a record of completed changes to finish correctly. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: Keeping everything feels safe, but unbounded accumulation overflows the window and degrades recall late in the run.
why_wrong.C: A bigger output budget allows longer answers, yet it cannot recover cleared results and adds nothing to retention.
why_wrong.D: Duplicating results looks protective, but it doubles token pressure and recreates the bloat clearing was meant to remove.

options.text: Add tool search so definitions load on demand instead of sending all schemas upfront.
Enable context editing to trim stale tool results once they stop being relevant.
Enable prompt caching because it removes cached tool definitions from the context window.
Collapse the whole toolset into one tool with a free-text argument to minimize schemas.
Repeat the full toolset definition after every assistant turn to refresh the model memory.

rationale: Tool search keeps definitions out of the window until needed, which fits large toolsets where most tools are idle each turn. Context editing removes old tool_result blocks from history, which fits long conversations where early results become dead weight. Each approach targets a different source of context pressure, so they compose.

source.excerpt: Tool search keeps tool definitions out of the context window until Claude asks for them.

stem: An operations agent exposes 60 tools and runs long troubleshooting sessions. Token analysis shows pressure from two sources: dozens of schemas loaded upfront, and stale tool results accumulating in history. Select TWO approaches that together BEST relieve both pressures.

why_wrong.C: Caching does cut what you pay for stable definitions, but cached tokens still occupy the window, so nothing shrinks.
why_wrong.D: One mega-tool seems lean, but a free-text argument destroys the typed schema the model relies on to call tools reliably.
why_wrong.E: Repeating definitions feels like a reminder, but it multiplies baseline tokens instead of reducing them.

options.text: Adopt the Strands harness, an assembled agent with tuned defaults that stays fully customizable.
Hand-write a custom agent loop from scratch to avoid depending on any framework defaults.
Encode the whole workflow as database stored procedures invoked by a cron schedule.
Run every request through one stateless prompt template with no tools or memory.

rationale: The Strands harness is a fully assembled agent with benchmarked defaults for system prompt, tools, memory, sessions, and context management, ready to take from idea to production. Because it is built on an open SDK, the team can still swap providers and override any default down to the primitives.

source.excerpt: Strands harness is a fully assembled, state-of-the-art agent harness.

stem: A startup team needs a production agent quickly: tuned defaults for prompt, tools, memory, and sessions, usable from a CLI or imported as a library, with freedom to swap model providers later. Which approach BEST fits?

why_wrong.B: Hand-rolling offers full control, but it burns team time rewiring exactly the harness pieces Strands already assembles.
why_wrong.C: Stored procedures suit fixed batch jobs, but they provide no model reasoning, tools, or session management for an agent.
why_wrong.D: A bare template is simple, yet without tools or memory it cannot act on systems or carry state across turns.

options.text: Call the specialist as a delegate agent from a parent tool, passing parent usage into the delegate run.
Chain the agents with a full hand-off so the parent ends and the specialist owns the run.
Run both agents independently and reconcile their separate usage reports afterwards.
Merge both agents into one agent with a doubled system prompt covering both roles.

rationale: In agent delegation the parent delegates work to another agent and takes back control when the delegate finishes, which matches the resume-control requirement. Passing the parent usage into the delegate run makes the final usage include both agents, giving single-run cost accounting and run-scoped cancellation.

source.excerpt: pass ctx.usage to the usage keyword argument of the delegate agent run so usage within that run counts towards the total usage

stem: A triage agent built with Pydantic AI must delegate ticket classification to a specialist agent, resume control afterwards to draft the reply, and report combined token usage for the whole run. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: A full hand-off fits fire-and-forget transfers, but here the parent must take back control after the delegate finishes.
why_wrong.C: Independent runs look flexible, but they break run-scoped usage accounting and cancellation that delegation provides.
why_wrong.D: Merging seems simpler, but it blends two roles into one prompt and forfeits the separation delegation gives.

options.text: Model the flow in LangGraph, mixing deterministic steps with agentic steps in one stateful graph.
Put the whole flow in a single LLM prompt and trust the model to apply the compliance rules.
Split the flow across cron scripts that pass state through filenames on a shared disk.
Remove the human approval step so the pipeline runs as one uninterrupted model call.

rationale: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration runtime for long-running, stateful agents that mixes deterministic hand-coded steps with LLM-driven steps in the same graph. Durable execution, persistence, and human-in-the-loop support cover the restart survival and approval requirements that a bare prompt cannot.

source.excerpt: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework and runtime for building, managing, and deploying long-running, stateful agents

stem: A bank builds a loan-processing agent: deterministic compliance checks and human approval steps must interleave with LLM-driven document analysis, and runs must survive restarts over several days. Which approach BEST fits?

why_wrong.B: One prompt is easy to write, but model memory is neither auditable nor deterministic enough for compliance gates.
why_wrong.C: Cron scripts can sequence jobs, but filename-passing gives no durable execution, streaming, or human-in-the-loop support.
why_wrong.D: Dropping approval simplifies the pipeline, yet it deletes a required control instead of orchestrating around it.

options.text: Move to graph-based control flow, orchestrating the specialists with an explicit state machine.
Keep nesting delegate agents inside tools until every branch has another layer.
Replace the specialists with a single agent and one model call per ticket.
Hard-code branch logic as string matching on each agent's free-text reply.

rationale: For the most complex multi-agent cases, a graph-based state machine controls execution across agents with explicit states and transitions. This makes conditional branches between specialists visible and auditable, which nested delegation layers and prose parsing cannot provide.

source.excerpt: for the most complex cases, a graph-based state machine can be used to control the execution of multiple agents

stem: A team outgrew simple delegation: their Pydantic AI support app now needs explicit states, conditional branches between specialist agents, and auditable transitions. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: More nesting reuses a familiar pattern, but deep delegate trees hide branch logic instead of making transitions explicit.
why_wrong.C: One agent reduces moving parts, but it collapses distinct specialists and states into an unauditable single step.
why_wrong.D: String matching on replies is quick to prototype, yet parsing prose to recover control decisions is brittle and opaque.
